blocks.text: The cerebrum has four major lobes (frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital). The lobar surface is heavily folded into sulci (valleys) and gyri (ridges); primary (major) sulci are more invariant in appearance than secondary (minor) sulci.

blocks.title: Major sulci/gyri and the function the notes assign to each
rows: Divides frontal lobe from parietal lobe
Divides frontal lobe from temporal lobe
Deep in the Sylvian fissure; sometimes regarded as the fifth lobe
Middle frontal gyrus (between superior and inferior frontal sulci)
Anterior cingulate gyrus (adjoining the cingulate sulcus, medial frontal lobe)
Inferior parietal lobe (angular and supramarginal gyri; interparietal sulcus separates superior and inferior parietal lobes)

blocks.title: Cortical localisation questions seen in the bank

items.text: **Q16**: the structure dividing frontal from temporal lobe is the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure); the central sulcus divides frontal from parietal.
**Q26**: primary sensory cortex = postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2); precentral gyrus is the distractor.
**Q46**: the motor cortex occupies the precentral gyrus (Brodmann area 4); the supplementary motor area (area 6) lies immediately anterior to the motor strip.

blocks.subtopic: Angular gyrus, arithmetic and Gerstmann syndrome
blocks.note: Notes only say the inferior parietal lobe (angular and supramarginal gyri) is important for visuospatial attention. **Q3** explanation adds: angular gyrus = normal arithmetical ability; Gerstmann syndrome = acalculia, finger agnosia, left/right confusion and agraphia, attributed to a lesion of the angular gyrus of the dominant parietal lobe. Not covered in the notes.

blocks.subtopic: Angular gyrus and language / nominal aphasia
blocks.note: **Q25** explanation: angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) is involved in processing auditory and visual input and language comprehension; lesions are associated with anomia. **Q24** localises nominal aphasia to the angular gyrus. The notes do not state this.

**Q13** explanation: the prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain regions to mature, with lesions producing disinhibition, apathy, loss of initiative and personality change. **Q43** explanation: it occupies nearly ==30%== of the brain. Neither is in the notes.

blocks.subtopic: Frontal lobe damage: forced utilisation and personality change
blocks.note: **Q19** explanation: damage to the orbitofrontal region can give forced utilisation behaviour. **Q34** (personality change, disinhibition, poor judgement, irritability) is answered frontal lobe. **Q31**: orbitofrontal cortex has a prominent role in social valuation and damage can cause a pseudopsychopathic syndrome. The notes only give orbitofrontal = associative learning and decision-making.

blocks.subtopic: Temporal lobe aura and mirror neurons
blocks.note: **Q22** explanation: epileptic aura arises from a circumscribed part of the temporal lobe (e.g. olfactory aura from the uncus). **Q52**: mirror neurons are in the inferior frontal (and superior parietal) cortex. Neither is in the notes.

bullets.text: Four lobes (frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital); folded into sulci (valleys) and gyri (ridges).
Central sulcus divides frontal from parietal lobe; lateral (Sylvian) sulcus divides frontal from temporal lobe; insula (deep in the Sylvian fissure) = primary gustatory cortex.
Precentral gyrus (frontal) = primary motor cortex; postcentral gyrus (parietal) = primary somatosensory cortex; both with a homunculus.
Middle frontal gyrus = dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (executive function); anterior cingulate = motivation; orbitofrontal cortex = associative learning and decision-making.

Superior temporal gyrus = primary auditory cortex; calcarine sulcus (medial occipital) = primary visual (striate) cortex; inferior parietal lobe (angular + supramarginal gyri) = visuospatial attention.

blocks.text: Most fundamental brain functions are represented bilaterally; higher associative functions usually lateralise to one hemisphere. Language comprehension is localised to the left temporal cortex while prosody (tonal modulation of speech) seems limited to the right hemisphere.

The hemisphere contralateral to the dominant hand is the dominant hemisphere and mediates language and speech functions. Dominance can be tested with Annette's handedness scale or the Edinburgh handedness inventory, but handedness is not always the same as dominance.

blocks.title: Hemisphere dominance by handedness (as stated in the notes)

blocks.subtopic: Left-handers and left language dominance: figures differ between notes and bank
blocks.note: Notes (p3) give ==64%== left / ~==20%== right / ==16%== bilateral for left-handers. **Q50** (and **Q8**) explanation states ==90%== of people are right-handed, ==99%== of right-handers have left-hemisphere language dominance, and of the ==10%== left-handers ==67%== have left-hemispheric language dominance (==33%== mixed or right). **Q50**'s keyed answer is 67; **Q8**'s keyed answer is 'most left handed individuals have left cerebral dominance'. Be aware of both figures.

blocks.text: Size asymmetry: the planum temporale is a triangular region on the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus, important for language processing, and larger on the left than the right hemisphere in ==65%== of brains. It is probably the most asymmetrical structure in the human brain, some individuals having a five times larger planum temporale on the left. This asymmetry is reportedly reduced or reversed (right>left) in schizophrenia.

blocks.title: Effects of left vs right hemisphere lesions (lists as printed in the notes)

blocks.text: Face recognition is listed in the same table as bilateral.

blocks.subtopic: Alexia with agraphia (Q7) and non-dominant hemisphere function (Q29)
blocks.note: **Q7** (left hemisphere lesion effect) is keyed 'alexia with agraphia': explanation says dominant (usually left) hemisphere lesions impair reading (acquired dyslexia), with right-sided motor deficits and agraphia. The notes' left-lesion list does not contain this. **Q29** is keyed 'pictorial memory' as a key function of the non-dominant hemisphere (picture memory predominantly affected by right brain injury) - also not in the notes.

bullets.text: Fundamental functions are bilateral; higher associative functions lateralise (language comprehension: left temporal; prosody: right).
Dominant hemisphere = contralateral to the dominant hand and mediates language/speech; tested by Annette's scale or Edinburgh inventory; handedness is not always dominance.
Right-handers: left dominant mostly, 10% right dominant. Left-handers: 20% right, 64% left, 16% bilateral (Q50 explanation gives 67% left).
Planum temporale: larger on the left in 65% of brains, most asymmetrical structure; reduced or reversed in schizophrenia.

Left lesions: aphasia, right-left disorientation, finger agnosia, aphasic dysgraphia, number-alexia dyscalculia, limb apraxia. Right lesions: visuospatial deficits, anosognosia, neglect, spatial dysgraphia/dyscalculia, constructional and dressing apraxia.

facts.label: Left-handers with right / left / bilateral dominance

sections.title: 3. Limbic system, Papez circuit and medial temporal structures

blocks.text: Broca first described the limbic lobe. Papez and later Maclean assigned the function of emotional processing to limbic structures, though this view is challenged in recent times.
The boundaries of the limbic system were subsequently expanded beyond the Papez circuit to include the amygdala, septum, basal forebrain, nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex.

The limbic system is thought to mediate emotional responses (through the amygdala), influence neuroendocrine responses (via the hypothalamus) and regulate the reward system (via the nucleus accumbens). It is often considered evolutionarily older than the higher cortical centres.

blocks.title: Medial temporal structures
rows: Include the hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex
Important role in memory processes; one of the few brain regions with continuous production of new neurons in adult life
Crucial for fear conditioning and emotional regulation

blocks.title: Papez / amygdala questions seen in the bank

items.text: **Q6**: hippocampus is in the Papez circuit; the explanation lists hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamic nucleus, cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus (distractors: temporal pole, medullary centre, trapezoid body, red nucleus).
**Q28**: Heschl's gyrus is **NOT** part of the Papez circuit (mammillary body, parahippocampal gyrus, cingulate gyrus and hippocampus are).

**Q5**: the false statement is 'learning does not occur without amygdala-mediated consolidation' - the explanation says learning and consolidation can occur despite amygdalar damage, while damage does cause loss of fear conditioning and (in monkeys) loss of maternal behaviour; the amygdala rates emotional importance and sets the level of hippocampal response.

blocks.subtopic: Dentate gyrus, entorhinal cortex and hippocampal blood supply
blocks.note: **Q17** (answer hippocampus): the dentate gyrus is the input region of the hippocampus and one of the few regions showing adult neurogenesis. **Q20**/**Q54** (answer temporal lobe / entorhinal cortex): the entorhinal cortex is one of the earliest regions affected in Alzheimer disease. **Q48**/**Q45**: the hippocampus (dentate gyrus) is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (with the anterior choroidal artery). The notes mention the entorhinal cortex and hippocampal neurogenesis only in the Papez/medial temporal context.

bullets.text: Papez circuit: hippocampus > fornix > mammillary bodies > mammillothalamic tract > anterior thalamic nucleus > genu of internal capsule > cingulate gyrus > parahippocampal gyrus > entorhinal cortex > perforant pathway > hippocampus.
Limbic boundaries expanded to amygdala, septum, basal forebrain, nucleus accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex.
Limbic roles: emotion (amygdala), neuroendocrine (hypothalamus), reward (nucleus accumbens); evolutionarily older than higher cortex.
Medial temporal structures: hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex.
Hippocampus: memory; continuous adult neurogenesis. Amygdala: fear conditioning and emotional regulation.

blocks.text: The basal ganglia are gray matter nuclei forming the largest subcortical structure in the brain. They are involved in planning and programming of movement and have a role in converting an abstract thought into voluntary action.

blocks.title: Components of the basal ganglia
rows: Functionally related to the basal ganglia but not considered part of the structure

blocks.text: The basal ganglia receive crucial inputs from the glutamatergic corticostriatal projection.

blocks.title: Basal ganglia dysfunction in disorders
rows: Volumetric changes and higher blood flow to the caudate nuclei; increased caudate metabolism in untreated subjects reduces after effective treatment
Degeneration of the striatum (mainly caudate nucleus) and selective loss of GABAergic neurons
Copper deposits in the lenticular nuclei
Acute bilateral anoxic damage to basal ganglia
Depigmentation of substantia nigra; Lewy bodies seen; striatal overactivity associated with bradykinesia
Progressive calcium deposition in the basal ganglia (early onset: schizophreniform psychoses and catatonia; later onset: dementia and choreoathetosis)

blocks.title: Basal ganglia questions seen in the bank

items.text: **Q2**: **OCD** is keyed to the lentiform nucleus - the explanation says caudate and lentiform nuclei dysfunction on **PET**; putamen + globus pallidus together form the lenticular/lentiform nuclei.
**Q44**: Huntington disease = degeneration of the striatum; the caudate shrinks dramatically, with rigidity and superimposed choreiform movements.
**Q51**: lesions of the subthalamic nucleus give hemiballismus (involuntary flailing, ballistic limb movements).

blocks.subtopic: Substantia nigra melanin; nucleus accumbens = ventral striatum
blocks.note: **Q23** (keyed substantia nigra): it contains melanin pigment, hence 'black substance'; it has two parts, one functionally equivalent to globus pallidus interna. **Q58** (keyed ventral striatum): nucleus accumbens forms the main part of the ventral striatum. The notes mention only **SN** depigmentation in Parkinsonism and nucleus accumbens as reward regulator.

bullets.text: Basal ganglia: largest subcortical gray matter structure; planning/programming of movement.
Striatum = caudate + putamen; pallidum = globus pallidus; putamen + globus pallidus = lenticular/lentiform nucleus. Subthalamic nuclei and substantia nigra are related but not part.
Glutamatergic corticostriatal input; Alexander's five circuits: motor, oculomotor, dorsolateral prefrontal (executive), anterior cingulate (motivation), lateral orbitofrontal (social intelligence).
OCD: caudate volume/blood-flow change; Tourette's: striatal dopaminergic dysfunction; Huntington: striatal (caudate) degeneration with loss of GABAergic neurons.

Wilson: copper in lenticular nuclei; CO poisoning: bilateral anoxic damage; hemiballismus: subthalamic nucleus damage; Parkinsonism: depigmented substantia nigra, Lewy bodies; Fahr's: calcium deposition.

blocks.text: The thalamus is a large oval mass of grey matter nuclei in the subcortical region, relaying all types of sensory information onto the cortex (except olfaction). It also relays cerebellar and basal ganglia inputs to the cerebral cortex, and is said to play a crucial role in filtering sensory information in preparation for cortical processing.

blocks.title: Thalamic nuclei mentioned in the notes
rows: Part of the limbic system; receives the mamillothalamic tract and fornix and connects to the cingulate cortex - relays information from hypothalamus and hippocampus onto the frontal cortex

blocks.subtopic: Visual pathway: lateral geniculate body and Meyer's loop
blocks.note: The notes say only that the optic nerve relays via the thalamus (geniculate body). **Q32** (keyed lateral geniculate body): optic radiations run from the lateral geniculate body to the occipital visual cortex. **Q41** (keyed temporal lobe): fibres detouring through the anterior temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) carry the contralateral superior quadrant, so damage gives contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopsia. Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Thalamus relays all sensory information to cortex except olfaction, plus cerebellar and basal ganglia inputs; filters sensory information.
Anterior thalamus (limbic): receives mamillothalamic tract and fornix, connects to cingulate cortex.
Pulvinar = visual attention; reticular nucleus generates sleep spindles.

blocks.text: The hypothalamus regulates physiological functions such as eating, drinking, sleeping and temperature regulation. It has chemoreceptors that respond to variations in glucose levels, osmolarity and acid balance, and plays a major role in neuroendocrine control.

blocks.title: Hypothalamic feeding centres
rows: Satiety centre; in animals, a lesion causes hyperphagia and obesity

blocks.text: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the brainstem and aids motor coordination by projecting climbing fibers to the contralateral cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

blocks.title: Cerebellar lesion vs inferior olivary lesion
rows: Ataxia and coarse intentional tremors, hypotonia, past pointing, pendular knee jerk
Appendicular ataxia due to motor incoordination

blocks.text: **Q42**: the satiety centre of the hypothalamus is the ventromedial hypothalamus (lateral hypothalamus = feeding centre; **VMH** lesion in animals gives hyperphagia and obesity).

bullets.text: Hypothalamus regulates eating, drinking, sleeping, temperature; chemoreceptors for glucose, osmolarity, acid balance; major neuroendocrine role.
Ventromedial hypothalamus = satiety centre (lesion in animals: hyperphagia, obesity); lateral hypothalamus = feeding centre.
Inferior olivary nucleus: brainstem; climbing fibers to contralateral cerebellar cortex via inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Inferior olivary lesion: contralateral appendicular ataxia, fails finger-nose test (mimics cerebellar lesion, which is ipsilateral).

blocks.text: The cerebellum prepares a motor plan and predicts the balance needed between muscle groups to carry out the intended action smoothly.

The role of the cerebellum in cognitive processes is increasingly appreciated. Cognitive dysmetria (Andreasen) refers to difficulty in coordinating and monitoring the receiving, processing and expressing of information, which could result from disrupted cortico-cerebellar circuitry in schizophrenia.

blocks.note: **Q30** (keyed cerebellum): extensive cerebellar damage causes 'scanning speech', a dysarthria with poor modulation, irregular cadence and inability to separate adjacent sounds. Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Cerebellum prepares the motor plan and predicts balance between muscle groups.
Lesions: ataxia, coarse intentional tremors, hypotonia, past pointing, pendular knee jerk.
Cognitive dysmetria (Andreasen): disrupted cortico-cerebellar circuitry in schizophrenia.

blocks.text: The brain stem is made of the midbrain, pons and medulla. Most of the cranial nerves (9 out of 12) enter or exit the brain from the brainstem.

blocks.title: Brain stem divisions
rows: Superior colliculi (conjugate gaze control) and inferior colliculi (auditory source localization); substantia nigra; periaqueductal grey matter (vocalization, freezing response to threat, pain suppression)
Positioned beneath the cerebellum; surrounds the upper half of the 4th ventricle
Surrounds the inferior part of the 4th ventricle; continuous with the spinal cord

blocks.title: Cranial nerves I-XII
rows: Runs on the basal surface of frontal cortex without passing through the thalamus; outgrowth of forebrain
Also an outgrowth of the forebrain; relays via thalamus (geniculate body)
Purely motor; supplies four of the six ocular muscles
Purely motor; supplies superior oblique (ocular muscle)
Both sensory and motor; transmits facial sensation, controls jaw muscles
Purely motor; supplies the lateral ocular muscle (printed as 'lateral abducens' in the notes; **Q18** explanation: lateral rectus)
Both sensory and motor; transmits taste sensation, controls facial muscles
As printed in the notes: Vestibular transmits auditory sensation; Cochlear transmits balance sensation
Motor control of pharynx; parasympathetic control of parotid gland; taste from back of tongue
Motor control of larynx and pharynx; parasympathetic control of viscera; visceral sensations

blocks.subtopic: Cranial nerve VIII labels look transposed in the notes
blocks.note: The notes' table prints 'Vestibular - transmits auditory sensation' and 'Cochlear - transmits balance sensation'; these functions are the reverse of the usual attribution but the notes are the only source here, so this is reproduced as printed. No question in the bank settles it (**Q18** lists 'Vestibulocochlear' as a nerve with sensory function). Verify against another source before relying on it.

blocks.mnemonic: Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet, Ah Heaven

blocks.title: Cranial nerve questions seen in the bank

items.text: **Q18**: abducens (**VI**) is the only purely motor nerve among the options (vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, olfactory, optic); it originates in the pons and innervates only the ipsilateral lateral rectus; impairment gives inward deviation without ptosis or pupil change.

**Q62**: oculomotor (**III**) is the purely motor cranial nerve (originates in the midbrain); impairment gives dilated pupil, ptosis and outward deviation, and impairs the efferent limb of the light and accommodation reflexes. Facial, vagus, glossopharyngeal and vestibulocochlear are the distractors.

blocks.note: **Q61** (keyed red nucleus): the mesencephalon (midbrain) includes the red nucleus. **Q60**: the ventral tegmental area is in the midbrain. Neither the red nucleus nor the **VTA**'s midbrain location is stated in the notes' brain stem paragraph.

bullets.text: Brain stem = midbrain, pons, medulla; 9 of 12 cranial nerves attach to it.
Midbrain: superior colliculi (gaze), inferior colliculi (auditory localisation), substantia nigra, periaqueductal grey (vocalization, freezing, pain suppression).
Pons lies beneath cerebellum, around upper 4th ventricle; medulla around lower 4th ventricle, continuous with spinal cord.
Purely motor: III (four of six ocular muscles), IV (superior oblique), VI (lateral ocular muscle). Mixed: V (face sensation, jaw), VII (taste, facial muscles).
IX: pharynx motor, parotid parasympathetic, posterior tongue taste. X: larynx/pharynx motor, visceral parasympathetic and sensation. XI: neck muscles. XII: tongue muscles.

facts.label: Ocular muscles supplied by the oculomotor nerve (III)

blocks.text: Unlike the cerebrum, where grey matter is on the outer surface, in the spinal cord grey matter occupies the deeper aspect forming an H-shaped column surrounding the **CSF**. White matter bundles form the anterior, lateral and dorsal columns around the grey matter.

blocks.title: Spinal cord columns
rows: Ascending spinothalamic tracts carrying touch, pressure, pain and temperature sensations

bullets.text: Spinal cord: grey matter deep, H-shaped, surrounding CSF; white matter outside (anterior, lateral, dorsal columns) - the reverse of the cerebrum.
Dorsal column = proprioception.
Anterior and lateral columns = ascending spinothalamic tracts (touch, pressure, pain, temperature).

blocks.text: **CSF** is secreted by the choroid plexus in the lateral, third and fourth ventricles at a rate of 300 ml/day, and is almost protein free.

blocks.title: CSF route
rows: Foramen of Magendie (single) and foramina of Luschka (two lateral)

blocks.text: The body of the lateral ventricle lies immediately below the corpus callosum, and the two lateral ventricles are separated by the septum pellucidum. The third ventricle lies between thalamus and hypothalamus; the fourth ventricle lies above the pons and just below the cerebellum.

blocks.title: Non-communicating vs communicating hydrocephalus
rows: Obstruction to **CSF** circulation, commonly within the third or fourth ventricle (foramen of Monroe)
Impaired **CSF** reabsorption in the subarachnoid space due to partial occlusion of the arachnoid villi

blocks.title: CSF questions seen in the bank

items.text: **Q10**: the septum pellucidum separates the two lateral ventricles (the body of the lateral ventricle lies immediately below the corpus callosum; the aqueduct of Sylvius is a distractor).
**Q12** and **Q57**: the foramen of Monro (interventricular foramen) connects the lateral ventricle(s) to the third ventricle.
**Q47**: **CSF** passes into the subarachnoid space via recesses in the fourth ventricle - foramina of Magendie and Luschka.

**Q53**: obstruction after basal brain trauma is most likely at the foramen of Monro - the explanation says it is the commonest site of block in non-communicating hydrocephalus, while the non-obstructive (communicating) form implicates arachnoid villi.

blocks.note: **Q10** explanation adds that an anomalous splitting of the septum pellucidum (cavum septum pellucidum) may be more common in schizophrenia than in the general population. Not in the notes.

bullets.text: CSF is made by the choroid plexus (lateral, third, fourth ventricles) at 300 ml/day, almost protein free.
Route: lateral > 3rd via foramina of Monroe; 3rd > 4th via aqueduct of Sylvius; 4th > subarachnoid space via Magendie (single) and Luschka (two lateral).
Lateral ventricles lie below the corpus callosum, separated by the septum pellucidum; third ventricle between thalamus and hypothalamus; fourth above the pons, below the cerebellum.
Obstruction (commonly third/fourth ventricle) = non-communicating hydrocephalus; impaired reabsorption via arachnoid villi = communicating hydrocephalus.

sections.title: 11. Blood supply to the brain: major branches

blocks.text: The internal carotid artery enters the circle of Willis and divides to form the anterior cerebral and middle cerebral arteries.

blocks.title: Arterial territories
rows: Medial and superior strip of the lateral aspect of the cerebral cortex, up to the parietal/occipital border
Most of the lateral aspect of the cerebral cortex, including Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the dominant hemisphere
Posterior cerebral artery (arises from basilar artery)
Inferomedial temporal lobe and the occipital lobe
Posterior inferior cerebellar arteries and anterior spinal branches of vertebral arteries
Basilar artery (runs along the midline of the pons)

blocks.title: TIA symptoms: carotid vs vertebrobasilar system
rows: Amaurosis fugax (due to blockade of retinal arteries); aphasia; hemiparesis; hemisensory loss; hemianopic visual loss
Diplopia, vertigo, vomiting; choking and dysarthria; ataxia; alexia without agraphia; hemisensory loss; hemianopic visual loss; transient global amnesia; tetraparesis; loss of consciousness (rare)

blocks.text: **Q15**: transient ischaemia of the carotid system produces aphasia (the carotid system supplies the language areas).

blocks.subtopic: Blood supply of the internal capsule
blocks.note: **Q1** (keyed Circle of Willis): the internal capsule contains the traversing corticospinal tract and is supplied by different parts of the circle of Willis - lenticulostriate branches of the **MCA**, and the recurrent artery of Heubner (**ACA**) for the inferior half of the anterior limb. The notes do not cover internal capsule supply.

bullets.text: ICA enters the circle of Willis and divides into ACA and MCA.
ACA: medial and superior strip of lateral cortex to the parietal/occipital border. MCA: most of lateral cortex incl. Broca's and Wernicke's (dominant hemisphere).
PCA (from basilar): inferomedial temporal lobe and occipital lobe. Medulla: PICA + anterior spinal branches. Pons: basilar artery.
Carotid TIA: amaurosis fugax, aphasia, hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, hemianopia.
Vertebrobasilar TIA: diplopia/vertigo/vomiting, choking and dysarthria, ataxia, alexia without agraphia, tetraparesis, transient global amnesia, rare LOC.

blocks.title: Arterial lesion syndromes
rows: Medial surface (ventromedial frontal lobe, cingulum, premotor cortex, medial motor strip)
Bilateral infarct: quadriparesis (legs weaker than arms) and akinetic mutism (ventromedial or cingulate syndrome)
Initially an agitated, confused state; evolves to akinesia, abulia, mutism and personality changes
Anterior branches of the upper division of the middle cerebral artery
Planning deficits, impaired working memory and apathy (**DLPFC** dysfunction)
Akinesia and personality change (orbitofrontal dysfunction) with a confabulatory amnesia resembling Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome

Wallenberg's lateral medullary syndrome: acute vertigo with cerebellar signs; ipsilateral face numbness, diplopia, nystagmus, Horner's syndrome and **IX**/X nerve palsy; contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss and mild hemiparesis

bullets.text: Bilateral ACA infarct: quadriparesis (legs weaker than arms) and akinetic mutism.
Recurrent artery of Huebner (head of caudate): agitation/confusion, then akinesia, abulia, mutism, personality change.
MCA upper-division anterior branches (lateral prefrontal): planning deficits, working-memory impairment, apathy (DLPFC).
Anterior communicating artery (basal forebrain): akinesia, orbitofrontal personality change, confabulatory amnesia resembling Wernicke-Korsakoff.
PICA thrombosis = Wallenberg's lateral medullary syndrome (ipsilateral face numbness, Horner's, IX/X palsy; contralateral spinothalamic loss).

blocks.title: Three major types of white matter pathway
rows: Run vertically, connecting higher and lower centres of the brain
Interconnect different regions within the same hemisphere
Interconnect similar regions in the opposite hemisphere

blocks.title: Commissures
rows: Largest bundle of fibres connecting the two cerebral hemispheres
Listed as a bundle (connection not specified)

blocks.text: The pericallosal artery, derived from the anterior cerebral artery, supplies the anterior aspect and most of the body of the corpus callosum. Left-sided apraxia and agnosia may be seen with vascular disruption.

The posterior cerebral artery territory supplies the splenium (posterior corpus callosum); disrupted supply prevents the right visual cortex accessing dominant-hemisphere processes such as language, resulting in alexia and colour anomia, with preserved ability to copy words because motor information is relayed via the anterior corpus callosum.

blocks.title: Named tracts
rows: Connects hippocampus to hypothalamus via mammillary bodies; relays cortical input to regulate neuroendocrine and autonomic systems
Major frontotemporal tract connecting orbitofrontal cortex to the anterior temporal lobes; important in social cognition and language

blocks.text: **Q14**: the artery supplying most of the corpus callosum is the anterior cerebral artery (rich supply from anterior cerebral and anterior communicating, also posterior cerebral; bilateral **ACA** occlusion infarcts both frontal lobes and the anterior corpus callosum).

bullets.text: Projection fibers vertical (higher-lower); association fibers within a hemisphere; commissural fibers between hemispheres.
Corpus callosum = largest commissure; others: anterior (olfactory bulbs), posterior (pretectal nuclei), hippocampal, habenular (posterior dorsal thalamic nuclei).
Pericallosal artery (from ACA) supplies anterior and most of the body of the corpus callosum; disruption: left-sided apraxia and agnosia.
PCA supplies the splenium; disruption: alexia and colour anomia with preserved word copying.

Fornix: hippocampus to hypothalamus via mammillary bodies. Arcuate fasciculus: Broca-Wernicke, damage = conduction aphasia. Uncinate fasciculus: OFC to anterior temporal lobe, social cognition and language.

blocks.text: The human brain contains approximately 10^11 neurons and approximately 10^12 glial cells (printed '1011' and '1012' in the notes; the superscript exponents appear to have lost their formatting). Brodmann divided the cortex into 47 'specialised' areas according to the distribution of neuron types (cytoarchitecture).

The neocortex (most of the cerebrum) has six layers, with the pial surface above layer 1 and white matter below layer 6. Layers 2 and 4 are mainly afferent (receiving inputs); layers 5 and 6 are mainly efferent (sending outputs).
Pyramidal neurons, with triangular cell bodies, make up nearly ==75%== of cortical neurons. Stellate cells (==25%==) are present in all layers except layer 1.

blocks.title: Neocortical layers
rows: Glial cells, dendrites from neurons of deeper layers and horizontal cells of Cajal
Granule cells and small pyramidal cells (larger as you move down)
Small and medium sized pyramidal cells
Some pyramidal cells, mostly granule cells; receives thalamocortical inputs
Largest pyramidal cells (esp. in motor cortex: Betz cells)
Mixture of all cells, spindle cells, Martinotti cells; major source of corticothalamic fibres; gives rise to association/commissural and projection fibres

blocks.title: Cortical cell questions seen in the bank

items.text: **Q21**: the most common neuron in the cerebral cortex is the pyramidal cell (about ==75%==; stellate ==25%==, in all layers except layer 1).

**Q63**: the most common cells of layer 4 (which receives thalamic input) are keyed as stellate cells; the explanation says stellate and fusiform cells lie in layer 4 and receive ascending thalamic fibres. The notes' layer table lists layer 4 as mostly granule cells - the bank keys stellate cells.

bullets.text: About 10^11 neurons and 10^12 glia; Brodmann: 47 areas by cytoarchitecture.
Neocortex has six layers; layers 2 and 4 mainly afferent, 5 and 6 mainly efferent.
Pyramidal cells ~75% of cortical neurons; stellate 25%, in all layers except 1.
Layer 4 (internal granular) receives thalamocortical input; layer 5 holds the largest pyramidal cells (Betz cells in motor cortex); layer 6 (multiform) is the main source of corticothalamic fibres.
Cerebellar cortex: molecular (basket, stellate), Purkinje, granular (granule, Golgi).

facts.label: Pyramidal / stellate share of cortical neurons

blocks.title: Special neuronal cell types
rows: GABAergic neurons located in the cerebellar cortex only; sole output of all motor coordination in the cerebellum, connecting to the deep cerebellar nuclei via inhibitory projections
Granular layer of the cerebellum, layer 4 of the cerebral cortex, dentate gyrus of the hippocampus, and olfactory bulb

Large pyramidal cells in layer 5 of the primary motor cortex; the largest neurons in the **CNS**, sometimes reaching 100 micrometres in diameter; about ==10%== of the pyramidal cell population in layer V of the human primary motor cortex
Layer **IV** of the cerebral cortex (from thalamus feeding forward to pyramidal cells) and also the cerebellum

blocks.title: Cell-type questions seen in the bank

items.text: **Q11**: Purkinje cells are uniquely found in the cerebellum (GABAergic, inhibitory projections to the deep cerebellar nuclei, sole output of cerebellar motor coordination).
**Q27**: Betz cells are the largest neurons in the human brain (layer V of the primary motor cortex, up to 100 micrometres, ~==10%== of layer V pyramidal cells).

blocks.subtopic: Neuron classification, electrical synapses, endosome, synaptogenesis
blocks.note: **Q4** (keyed amacrine neurons): neurons are classed by size as Golgi type 1 (long axon), Golgi type 2 (short axon) and amacrine neurons (no axon). **Q64** (keyed retina): electrical synapses (gap junctions) are abundant in the retina and cerebral cortex. **Q55**: an endosome recycles cell membrane. **Q59**: synaptogenesis peaks in the first two postnatal years. None of these is in the notes.

**Q36** (telencephalon gives rise to the cerebral hemispheres: cortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia), **Q39** (diencephalon = thalamus, subthalamus, hypothalamus) and **Q37** (neural crest arises from the dorsal neural tube) test embryology, which the notes do not cover.

bullets.text: Purkinje cells: GABAergic, cerebellar cortex only, sole output of cerebellar motor coordination (inhibitory to deep nuclei).
Granule cells: cerebellar granular layer, cortical layer 4, hippocampal dentate gyrus, olfactory bulb.
Betz cells: large pyramidal cells in layer 5 of primary motor cortex; largest CNS neurons (up to 100 micrometres); ~10% of layer V pyramidal cells.
Stellate cells: layer IV of cerebral cortex (thalamus to pyramidal cells) and cerebellum.

facts.label: Betz cells share of layer V pyramidal cells

blocks.text: Glial cells have supportive metabolic functions and also modulate neuronal function, e.g. via production of neurosteroids. The notes say there are 3 types but go on to list four (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells described as 'a special type of glia').

blocks.title: Glial cells
rows: Most numerous; star-shaped; enable nutrition of neurons, break down some neurotransmitters, maintain the blood-brain barrier
Seen in the **CNS** (replaced by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves); produce myelin sheaths that help saltatory conduction and quicken signal transmission
Descendants of macrophages; scavenger cells that clear neuronal debris following cell death
Cover the ventricles and facilitate **CSF** circulation via their ciliary processes

blocks.title: Glial cell questions seen in the bank

items.text: **Q9**: microglia are the descendants of macrophages clearing neuronal debris (astrocytes: nutrition, deactivating neurotransmitters, blood-brain barrier; oligodendrocytes in **CNS** and Schwann cells in **PNS** myelinate).
**Q35**: forming the **CNS** myelin sheath is **NOT** an astrocyte function (that is the oligodendrocyte).
**Q38**: Schwann cells are the neuroglia present in the peripheral nervous system.
**Q56**: myelination is the oligodendrocyte function (not metabolic clearance of transmitters, gliosis, structural support or blood-brain barrier contribution).

blocks.note: **Q33** (keyed 'mesodermal in origin'): evidence supports a mesodermal origin of microglia, which therefore share features with myeloid cells. **Q49** (keyed glutamate dehydrogenase): this enzyme is seen only in astrocytes. Neither is in the notes.

bullets.text: Glia: supportive and metabolic; modulate neurons (e.g. neurosteroids).
Astrocytes: most numerous, star-shaped; neuronal nutrition, breakdown of some neurotransmitters, blood-brain barrier.
Oligodendrocytes: CNS myelin (Schwann cells in PNS); saltatory conduction.
Microglia: macrophage descendants, scavenge neuronal debris. Ependymal cells: line ventricles, ciliary action aids CSF circulation.

blocks.text: The blood-brain barrier is located in the endothelial cells of brain capillaries. Unlike endothelial cells elsewhere, brain endothelial cells have tight junctions with high electrical resistance, providing an effective barrier against molecules. Brain capillaries are also in contact with foot processes of astrocytes that separate the capillaries from the neurons.

blocks.title: What crosses the barrier
rows: Penetrate relatively easily via the lipid membranes of the cells
Unable to cross without specialised carrier-mediated transport mechanisms

blocks.text: Inflammation such as meningitis weakens the blood-brain barrier.
Some brain areas lack a blood-brain barrier - the circumventricular organs, e.g. subfornical organ, area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone), median eminence and posterior pituitary.

**Q40**: lipophilic substances penetrate the barrier better; endothelial cells are joined by tight junctions (not gap junctions); inflammation weakens (not strengthens) the barrier; the barrier is formed by endothelial cells, not microglial foot processes; the basal forebrain is not named as lacking the barrier.

bullets.text: BBB sits in brain capillary endothelial cells with tight junctions of high electrical resistance, plus astrocyte foot processes.
Lipid-soluble molecules (ethanol, caffeine) cross easily; water-soluble ions (Na, K) need carrier-mediated transport.
Inflammation (meningitis) weakens the barrier.
No barrier at circumventricular organs: subfornical organ, area postrema, median eminence, posterior pituitary.

blocks.title: Dopaminergic pathways by length
rows: Amacrine cells in the retina and the olfactory system

blocks.text: The nigrostriatal pathway is the extrapyramidal pathway crucial for motor control and accounts for most of the brain's dopamine.

blocks.title: Dopamine pathways: origin, destination and effect of blockade
rows: Substantia nigra to striatum and amygdala via medial forebrain bundle
**DA** deficiency (e.g. Parkinson's) or blockade by antipsychotics can cause extrapyramidal side effects
Ventral tegmental area (**VTA**) to nucleus accumbens and hippocampus via medial forebrain bundle
Blockade produces the desirable antipsychotic effect by controlling positive psychotic symptoms
**VTA** to cingulate cortex and prefrontal regions via medial forebrain bundle
Low **DA** or **DA** blockade associated with negative symptoms (alogia, anhedonia, amotivation, apathy)
Hypothalamus to pituitary via portal vessels
Dopamine acts as **PIH** (prolactin inhibitory hormone); blockade increases prolactin
Disturbed thermoregulation and possibly weight gain

blocks.subtopic: Location of the ventral tegmental area
blocks.note: **Q60** (keyed midbrain): the **VTA** lies medial to the substantia nigra in the midbrain, and its dopaminergic neurons give rise to the mesocorticolimbic system (mesoaccumbens pathway = reward). The notes name the **VTA** as the origin of the mesolimbic/mesocortical tracts but do not state its location.

bullets.text: Long paths: nigrostriatal, mesocortical, mesolimbic; short: tuberoinfundibular, incertohypothalamic; ultrashort: retinal amacrine cells and olfactory system.
Nigrostriatal (SN to striatum): motor control, most brain dopamine; DA deficiency/blockade causes extrapyramidal effects.
Mesolimbic (VTA to nucleus accumbens/hippocampus): blockade = antipsychotic effect on positive symptoms.
Mesocortical (VTA to cingulate/prefrontal): low DA or blockade = negative symptoms.
Tuberoinfundibular: dopamine is PIH, blockade raises prolactin; incertohypothalamic: thermoregulation, possibly weight gain.

blocks.title: Cholinergic pathways
rows: Innervates thalamic relay neurons and reticular nuclei; part of the **ARAS** (ascending reticular activating system), important to maintain wakefulness and **REM** sleep
Projects to hippocampus, frontal cortex and amygdala; degeneration implicated in Alzheimer's disease

blocks.text: Most of the brain's serotonergic neurons originate in the midbrain dorsal and median raphe nuclei and ascend to innervate the entire cortex, basal ganglia and thalamus, and also descend to the spinal cord.

The noradrenergic projection originates at the locus coeruleus (pons) and ascends to most of the cortex via the medial forebrain bundle; like the serotonin system, it also descends to the spinal cord.

bullets.text: Cholinergic brainstem pathway (pedunculopontine, laterodorsal tegmental nuclei) = part of ARAS: wakefulness and REM sleep.
Cholinergic basal forebrain pathway: nucleus basalis of Meynert to hippocampus, frontal cortex, amygdala; degenerates in Alzheimer's.
Serotonin: dorsal and median raphe nuclei (midbrain) to cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus and spinal cord.
Noradrenaline: locus coeruleus (pons) to most of the cortex via medial forebrain bundle, and to the spinal cord.

blocks.text: Glutamate is the most common excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, so almost all cortical descending tracts (from pyramidal cells) use it; this large corticofugal output makes up most of the corona radiata. All association and commissural fibres are glutamatergic, as are many thalamic neurons (so thalamocortical projections too).
Cerebellar output from deep nuclei, subthalamic nuclei to globus pallidus projections, and brainstem-to-spinal cord projections are also predominantly glutamatergic.

**GABA** is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. Unlike other transmitters, there are no specific neurochemical pathways where **GABA** dominates; it is the major transmitter of cerebral interneurons, which are ubiquitous throughout the cortex.
Interneurons are usually short neurons connecting two other neurons; they carry neither motor nor sensory information but modulate local neural circuitry.

blocks.title: Cortical GABAergic interneuron subtypes
rows: About ==40%== of all interneurons; reduced frontal cortex expression is a well-replicated feature of schizophrenia; two subtypes: basket cells and chandelier cells
==30%== of interneurons; also called Martinotti cells
Receive direct thalamocortical input; synapse with soma or dendrites of pyramidal neurons; provide excitatory-inhibitory balance
Synapse with the proximal axonal hillock of pyramidal neurons; may have an overall excitatory role by short-circuiting action potential propagation, though the role is still unclear

bullets.text: Glutamate = most common excitatory transmitter: cortical descending tracts (most of corona radiata), association and commissural fibres, many thalamic neurons (thalamocortical).
Also glutamatergic: cerebellar deep-nuclei output, subthalamic nuclei to globus pallidus, brainstem to spinal cord.
GABA = primary inhibitory transmitter; no dominant GABA pathway - major transmitter of cortical interneurons.
Two cortical interneuron subtypes: parvalbumin (~40%) and somatostatin (30%, Martinotti cells).
PV interneuron reduction in frontal cortex is a replicated finding in schizophrenia; PV types: basket cells (thalamocortical input, E-I balance) and chandelier cells (axonal hillock).
